newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean central bank says big bank not in trouble.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean central bank says big bank not in trouble.

text.p: South Korea's central bank, seeking to calm fears that a second big corporate collapse this year could fuel a banking crisis, denied on Thursday that a leading financial institution was in trouble.
Korea First Bank is the main creditor of Sammi Steel Co, which defaulted on debts on Wednesday, a day after filing for court protection.
The bank also has the most exposure to Hanbo Steel Co, which collapsed in January with debts of $5.8 billion in the country's biggest corporate failure.
"Korea First Bank has no funding problem at all despite Sammi," said Park Chul, director of the central bank's monetary policy division.
"As it is one of the nation's biggest banks, it can handle the Sammi case," he said in an interview.
Park denied media reports that the central bank planned emergency loans to the bank.
The European rating agency IBCA said on Wednesday it had downgraded the individual ratings of Korea First Bank, Cho Hung Bank and Korea Exchange Bank
An IBCA statement said the impact on Korea First of the Hanbo failure "will be considerable" and added that the bank's downgrading reflected its exposure to Sammi.

Stocks edged lower after a sharp fall on Wednesday on fears the Sammi failure could have a knock-on effect on other struggling companies by further raising borrowing costs and making banks more cautious about lending.
The leading index lost 3.43 points to end at 642.86.
A central bank official said the failure of two big steelmakers and almost a month of labour strikes had dashed hopes for an economic revival in South Korea this year.
The bank had lowered estimates for gross domestic product (GDP) growth this year to 6.0 percent from 6.4 percent, deputy bank governor Kim Young-dae told reporters.
"Strikes in January, the Hanbo collapse and Sammi's failure have all had a negative impact on the economy," Kim said.
"Previously, we thought the economy would rebound in the second half of this year. But that possibility has fizzled."
Sammi Steel was staggering under liabilities of 1.45 trillion won ($1.64 billion) at the end of 1996 against assets of 1.53 trillion won, according to company figures.
Korea First Bank had 217.4 billion won of outstanding loans to Sammi Steel as of Monday, down from 395.9 billion at the end of 1996, according to bank figures.
Kwon Woo-ha, the bank's managing director, said only 130 billion won of those loans was unsecured.
"But the bank is so big, with assets of 4.8 trillion won, so we can handle Sammi's problem," he said in an interview.
"We're not worried about the Sammi case," he said. "It will not damage our management. I'm very positive about that."

Financial analysts said Sammi's collapse highlighted a mountain of bad debt amassed by domestic banks after decades of reckless lending. They said foreign lenders were now shying away from South Korean financial institutions.
"Foreign banks that said they would offer us loans last week suddenly turned their backs on us today," said a loans manager at a leading domestic bank.

South Korean banks funded the nation's rise to economic "tiger" status from the ashes of World War Two, extending loans to politically-favoured companies in their role as virtual government cashiers. (Conversion US$1 = 884.40 won)
